title: Accelerating bainitic transformation and enhancing mechanical properties by chemical heterogeneity in ultrafine bainitic steel
abstract: This study employed a processing route (CPBT) integrating a cold-rolled pearlite precursor with rapid heating to regulate bainitic transformation and mechanical properties of ultrafine bainitic steel. The results indicated that the bainitic transformation was significantly accelerated by the CPBT treatment, promoted by both an increased density of nucleation sites from cold-rolling-induced grain refinement and preferential nucleation in Mn-/Cr-depleted austenite regions. The enhanced transformation kinetics also resulted in a pronounced refinement of blocky retained austenite. Furthermore, the CPBT process introduced chemically heterogeneous bainite, characterized by refined bainitic ferrite laths and thickened Mn-/Cr-enriched film-like retained austenite, in contrast to the elemental homogeneity of conventional bainite. This microstructure improved tensile strength through grain refinement strengthening, while the sustained transformation-induced plasticity effect from the chemically heterogeneous retained austenite during deformation enhanced elongation.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Owing to the outstanding combination of strength, toughness and fatigue resistance, considerable research attention has been devoted to ultrafine bainitic steels  [1–3] . Nevertheless, the extended austempering duration and the suboptimal strength-toughness balance restrict wider engineering implementation. Increasing the nucleation density coupled with enhancing the transformation driving force has been established as a key methodology for reducing the phase transformation duration  [4–7] .

Advanced heat treatment processes, such as tailored alloying  [8,9]  and multi-stage thermomechanical treatments  [10–13] , can accelerate bainitic transformation kinetics. However, this benefit is often achieved at the expense of higher alloy costs and more complex process controls, which represents a critical limitation. The mechanical behavior of ultrafine bainitic steels is primarily dictated by the dimensions and phase fraction of bainitic ferrite (BF). Meanwhile, the heterogeneous phase transformation in stability-graded retained austenite (RA) significantly impedes necking propagation, thereby enhancing the synergy between ductility and toughness  [14–16] . Hence, tailoring refined BF laths along with metastable RA that exhibits a sustained transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect is a key to achieving superior comprehensive mechanical properties.

Previous studies have demonstrated that controlling microscale chemical heterogeneity can effectively modulate bainitic transformation and improve mechanical properties. Specifically, intercritical annealing with Mn partitioning or the creation of chemically patterned austenite can introduce elemental heterogeneity prior to bainitic transformation  [17–21] . This heterogeneity serves to accelerate the bainitic transformation rate and simultaneously enables the formation of multi-scale RA, resulting in synergistic mechanical enhancement. In this study, a novel phase transformation pathway design based on chemical heterogeneity is proposed to break the trade-off between rapid processing and premium strength-toughness performance in ultrafine bainitic steels, thereby targeting the dual optimization of manufacturing efficiency and mechanical excellence.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs:
A steel with a nominal composition of Fe-0.32C-2.2Si-1.7Mn-1.9Cr-1.0Ni (in wt%) was melted in a vacuum induction melting furnace, homogenized at 1200 °C for 12 h and hot-rolled into a 6-mm-thick plate. Regarding the novel strategy outlined in  
                      Fig. 1 (a), the initial pearlite was generated by furnace cooling from 930 °C to an isothermal transformation temperature of 650 °C and holding for 4 h, followed by cold rolling to a 70 % thickness reduction. Subsequently, the cold-rolled pearlite was rapidly heated to 930 °C at a rate of ∼100 °C/s, held for 3 s for austenitization, then transferred to 340 °C and held for 0.5 and 1.5 h to achieve bainitic transformation, followed by cooling to room temperature (abbreviated as CPBT-0.5 and CPBT-1.5). As a conventional counterpart ( Fig. 1 b), samples taken from the hot-rolled plate underwent the identical austempering procedure under slow heating (20 °C/s) and prolonged soaking conditions (15 min), which are referred to as CBT-0.5 and CBT-1.5, respectively. Dilatometric analysis was conducted on a Bähr DIL-805 quenching dilatometer with rectangular specimens of 4 mm in width and 10 mm in length to quantitatively evaluate the bainitic transformation kinetics. For the tensile testing sheets, high- and low-temperature salt bath furnaces were employed for rapid heating and isothermal bainitic transformation, respectively, while a muffle furnace was used for slow heating.

Microstructural observations were conducted using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Microstructure morphology and concentration profiles of Mn/Cr were characterized using a scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) fitted with energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). The volume fraction of RA was determined using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation over a 2θ range of 47° to 93°. Flat tensile specimens (gauge dimensions: 25 × 6 × 1.5 mm³) were tested on an MTS 810 universal testing machine at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min. All measurements were repeated at least three times to confirm reproducibility.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs:
From the dilatometry curves shown in  
                      Fig. 2 (a), the incubation period, completion time and bainitic transformation rate were determined. Notably, the CPBT sample markedly accelerated transformation kinetics compared to the CBT reference, with the incubation period reduced by 90 % (from 270 s to 25 s) and the completion time decreased by 40 % (from 4700 s to 2800 s). The CPBT process led to the completion of the bainitic transformation within 0.5 h. The dilatation-time curves also showed that the CPBT-1.5 and CBT-1.5 samples exhibited the same change in relative length and thus contained the identical amount of bainite. This similarity was predominantly ascribed to the identical austempering temperature.

Fig. 2 (b) and (c) show the XRD patterns and corresponding volume fraction of each phase in the CBT and CPBT samples. The volume fractions of RA in CBT-1.5, CPBT-0.5 and CPBT-1.5 were determined to be 14.6 ± 1.8 %, 15.1 ± 1.0 % and 14.5 ± 1.2 %, respectively, with no significant differences observed among these groups. The remaining portion constituted the formed BF. In contrast, the volume fraction in CBT-0.5 was significantly lower, at only 10.2 % ± 1.6 %. The formed BF in the CBT-0.5 sample was estimated by dilatation comparison. Accordingly, the fresh martensite (FM) fraction was calculated as the difference between the untransformed undercooled austenite fraction and the total RA fraction measured by XRD. This was due to insufficient enrichment of elements in RA during the relatively short austempering time, which resulted in the transformation of RA to martensite upon cooling to room temperature.

As shown in  
                      Fig. 3 (a 1 ) and (b 1 ), the observed microstructure of the CBT-1.5 sample consisted of lamellar BF laths and film-like RA as well as blocky RA, as frequently reported in ultrafine bainitic microstructures  [22,23] . Meanwhile, no microscopic partitioning of Mn and Cr was detected at both the BF lath/blocky RA (d 1 ) and the BF lath/film-like RA (d 2 ) interfaces from the EDS line scans. As shown in  Fig. 3 (a 2 ), in addition to the homogeneous bainite similar to that found in the CBT-1.5 sample, the CPBT-1.5 sample also contained chemically heterogeneous bainite (HB). The HB presented a pearlite-like morphological structure, including lamellar and quasi-spherical forms. An examination of  Fig. 3 (b₂) revealed that the lamellar HB consisted of Mn-/Cr-depleted BF alongside Mn-/Cr-enriched RA. A significant variation in Mn and Cr concentration across the lamellae was observed (d 3 ). The strong gradient of Mn and Cr contents mainly originated from heterogeneous high-temperature austenite transformed from cold-rolled pearlite  [6,24] . Rapid heating suppressed the long-range diffusion of alloying elements in austenite. Consequently, the high-temperature austenite inherited the substantial concentration gradient of the cold-rolled pearlite, thereby forming a mixed microstructure comprising high-alloy austenite (from dissolved Mn-/Cr-enriched cementite) and low-alloy austenite (from transformed Mn-/Cr-depleted ferrite). By nucleating preferentially in the low-alloy austenite, bainite gained an increased driving force for transformation. The high-alloy austenite was retained upon cooling to room temperature due to its superior stability, forming Mn-/Cr-enriched film-like RA.

Fig. 3  also presents the thickness distributions of BF laths and film-like RA, as well as the equivalent diameter of blocky RA, measured from TEM and SEM images. The average BF lath thickness was 199 ± 22 nm for the CBT sample, compared to 163 ± 19 nm for the CPBT sample ( Fig. 3 (e 1 )). The corresponding values for the film-like RA were 66 ± 16 nm and 92 ± 15 nm, respectively ( Fig. 3 (e 2 )). In contrast to the CBT sample, the CPBT sample demonstrated a noticeable leftward shift in the Gaussian fitting curve peak for BF laths, implying a reduction in average thickness. The film-like RA, however, showed an opposing trend with a rightward peak shift. BF lath refinement resulted from the accelerated bainitic transformation kinetics arising from Mn-/Cr-depleted regions in heterogeneous austenite and prior austenite grain refinement from cold rolling. Meanwhile, the thicker film-like RA, characterized by Mn/Cr enrichment, mainly originated from the cementite in the cold-rolled pearlite  [25] . A comparative analysis revealed that the CPBT sample possessed more refined and uniform blocky RA than the CBT sample. This refinement exhibited a predominant size distribution of 1.0–2.2 μm, with a substantially lower average value of 1.33 ± 0.52 μm ( Fig. 3 (e 3 )).

According to the morphology and orientation relationship between BF laths and prior austenite, IPF maps of prior austenite for CBT and CPBT ( 
                      Fig. 4 (a) and (e)) were reconstructed and shown in  Fig. 4 (b) and (f). The average prior austenite grain size (PAGS) of CPBT was calculated as 8.6 ± 2.2 μm, far below that of the CBT sample at 14.6 ± 2.7 μm. The extensive cold deformation enhanced austenite nucleation through the generation of high-density dislocations and an increased number of grain boundaries. Following rapid heating and a short isothermal hold, ultrafine-grained austenite developed, which increased the bainite nucleation sites and thereby accelerated the bainitic transformation  [26] .  Fig. 4 (c) and (g) present band contrast (BC) maps superimposed with phase maps. Quantitative EBSD analysis indicated RA fractions of 10.0 % and 5.0 % for the CBT and CPBT samples, respectively, both of which were lower than the corresponding values calculated via XRD ( Fig. 2 (c)). The underestimation of RA content by EBSD primarily stems from its inherent limitations, including a restricted analysis area and insufficient resolution for detecting minute RA constituents  [27] .  Fig. 4 (d) and (h) show the misorientation angle distribution, with low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) defined as 2° to 15° and high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) exceeding 15°. Based on calculations, the CPBT sample contained a larger proportion of LAGBs (54 %) than the CBT sample (29 %), which could be attributed to the refinement of the BF laths and PAGS.

Fig. 5  shows the tensile responses of samples under different treatment conditions. The CBT-0.5 sample exhibited the highest strength but the lowest elongation, which was primarily attributed to the fresh martensite formed from the incomplete bainitic transformation. Conversely, CPBT samples demonstrated superior elongation to their CBT counterparts. The improved ductility originated from the sustained TRIP effect, which was enabled by the refined blocky and coarsened film-like RA with Mn/Cr enrichment. This mechanism was demonstrated by the marked reduction in RA fraction during interrupted tensile tests ( Fig. 5 (a)) and the corresponding instantaneous work hardening response ( Fig. 5 (b)). The CPBT-1.5 sample exhibited similar ultimate tensile strength to the CPBT-0.5 sample. As can be seen from the mechanical property radar chart presented in  Fig. 5 (c), the CPBT sample after austempering for 1.5 h exhibited a superior product of strength and elongation (PSE) value (29.6 GPa·%) that generally met the standards of third-generation advanced high-strength steels.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The rapid heating process applied to a cold-rolled initial pearlite microstructure accelerated the bainitic transformation and yielded a chemically heterogeneous bainite, characterized by alternating Mn-/Cr-enriched film-like RA and Mn-/Cr-depleted BF laths. This accelerated mechanism originated from the increased nucleation sites provided by cold-rolling-induced grain refinement, combined with preferential nucleation within Mn-/Cr-depleted regions of the high-temperature austenite. Consequently, the refinement of BF laths, coupled with the sustained TRIP effect from the chemically heterogeneous RA, enhanced the mechanical properties of the ultrafine bainitic steel.
